 USU Faculty Awarded NSF RAPID Grant for Earthquake Research 
 By Chalyce MacDonald | November 19, 2026 
Full Size 
 A research team poses for a photo on an earthquake fault in Panama on Nov. 19. Pictured are Assistant Professor Kelian Dascher-Cousineau (top), doctoral student Quincey Nielson (bottom-left), and Alba Rodriguez-Padilla (bottom-right). (Photo credit: Alba Rodriguez-Padilla)
 × 
Download 
 Close 
 Download 
 A Utah State University researcher has been awarded Rapid Response Research grant funds from the U.S. National Science Foundation to collect time-sensitive earthquake data.
 Alba M. Rodriguez Padilla, an assistant professor from USU’s Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences , will be conducting field research on the magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck the Azuero Peninsula in southern Panama on Oct. 9.
 “We’re going to map … the locations where the fault pierced the surface, to figure out what is the geometry of the fault system that hosted this earthquake,” Rodriguez Padilla said, adding that the data is “perishable in the sense that it’s just cracked dirt and rocks — and it rains a lot in Panama, so that information is being erased constantly.”
 Among her current work, Rodriguez Padilla studies factors which make earthquakes grow large enough to threaten infrastructure and lifelines, including transfers between faults. She said this earthquake in Panama is peculiar.
 “One of the big assumptions in our seismic hazard models … in the Western United States is that earthquakes will preferentially happen on fast-slipping, mature faults,” she said. “In Panama, the earthquake started on of these faults — then, on one of its ends, it decided to travel to another fault instead of continuing on this very well-positioned fault for hosting the earthquake. Then, on the other end it did exactly the same thing. So, it’s an earthquake that broke the rules. That’s why we’re interested in it.”
 Data collected during this project will also contribute to research conducted by USU professors Alexis Ault and Dennis Newell, regarding CO2 flux measurements and changes in fault permeability following an earthquake.
 Rodriguez Padilla and her team of other faculty, postdocs, and grad students will be carrying out their research in mid-November with plans for a second field effort in January.
